I just wanted to defend the electoral college (despite my disappointment of Bush winning some time back). Especially since it is inevitably going to probably be under attack again (if, indeed, the true final tally shows that Hillary won the popular vote).

The electoral college is a crucial component of the United States' system of check and balances. In particular, it is a component of the balance between the federal government and the individual States. It gives much more swing to the individual States; and if we hadn't made the seventeenth amendment, then the electoral college would make even more sense. Since then the Senate would represent the concerns of the State governments, the House of the people, and the electoral college would elect the President as a decent mediator. Regardless, however, If it weren't for the electoral college, then power would have been centralized a lot sooner in the U.S. than has actually come to pass. In short, by incorporating such power to the populace of the individual states, it helps decentralize political power.

I would argue that this is probably also why the United States didn't develop like almost every other country in the Americas: loosely populated land with a handful of quite small cities followed by almost the entire population living in the capital-turned-megalopolis, and the notable disadvantages of such centralization of the entire country(and not just politically speaking) of that occurring (incidentally, this is why I eye the 23rd amendment with suspicion on a cold night). Or the development of a small densely-populated district in said megalopolis basically deciding the entire election.

Tl;dr: the electoral college decentralizes political power and is an important check and balance. Don't throw it out.
